# `silk/system/system_clock_native`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

The native provider of the `SystemClock` effect: the time of day, as seconds since 1970.

## When to use
Provide [`OsSystemClock`](#OsSystemClock) for `SystemClock` in a native program, for timestamps. In a test,
provide a fake that returns a fixed time.

## Details
Each call reads the real-time clock of the system. A failure of the clock is a trap.

## Gotchas
- This clock can go back when the system time is set. Use `silk.system.monotonic_clock_native` to measure
  durations.
- On Linux, it needs glibc 2.17 or later.
- The provider exists on WASI, Darwin on aarch64, and Linux with GNU libc on x86_64 or aarch64.

## Examples
### Read the time
```silk
import silk.core.effect { Effect }
import silk.system.system_clock_native { OsSystemClock }
import silk.system.system_clock { Instant, SystemClock }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut clock = OsSystemClock.make()
  let now = run SystemClock.now() |> Effect.provideMut<SystemClock>(&mut clock)

  // Seconds since 1970. 1600000000 is in September 2020.
  let nanoseconds = SystemClock.nanoseconds(&now)
  if SystemClock.seconds(&now) < 1600000000 || nanoseconds < 0 || nanoseconds >= 1000000000 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `OsSystemClock` with `import silk.system.system_clock_native { OsSystemClock }`.

pub struct OsSystemClock

The native `SystemClock` provider: the time of day, as seconds since 1970. It has no state. A
failure is a trap.

### Gotchas
- This clock can go back when the system time is set. Use `silk.system.monotonic_clock_native` to
  measure durations.
- On Linux, it needs glibc 2.17 or later.
